q.q: Which is the best one-mark definition of a communication protocol?
o: An agreed set of rules that lets different devices communicate
A standard that sets the speed of every network cable
A program that sends data from one device to another
A set of rules for how a network should be laid out
q.why: A full definition needs both ideas: rules, and different devices communicating.

q.q: Which is NOT normally defined by a communication protocol?
o: The error detection method
The colour of the network cable
The format of each message
How devices authenticate
q.why: Protocols set rules for data exchange: format, authentication, error handling and so on, not cable colours.

q.q: Why are protocols needed for devices from different manufacturers?
o: The devices may differ in hardware, software, speed and character set
Each device must have the same operating system
Devices from different makers cannot share one cable
Each manufacturer's devices use a different topology
q.why: Protocols give interoperability: devices that differ in technology can still exchange data if they follow the same rules.

q.q: Which body manages the radio-frequency spectrum and writes recommendations that standardise telecommunications worldwide?
o: W3C
ITU
IETF
IEEE
q.why: The ITU is the UN agency for telecommunications, including spectrum and satellite orbits.

q.q: What is the main aim of the W3C?
o: Setting LAN standards such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi
Publishing the internet protocols TCP and IP
Managing the radio spectrum and satellite orbits
Developing open web standards so the web works for everyone
q.why: The W3C develops web protocols and guidelines such as HTML and CSS, its 'One Web' aim.

q.q: Which body sets LAN standards such as Ethernet (802.3) and Wi-Fi (802.11)?
o: W3C
ITU
ISO
IEEE
q.why: The IEEE sets LAN standards; ISO published the OSI model.

q.q: Which body publishes the internet's protocols such as TCP, IP and HTTP?
o: IETF
IEEE
ISO
ITU
q.why: The Internet Engineering Task Force publishes internet protocols.

q.q: How do protocols make data transmission more reliable?
o: They store a backup copy of all data on each device
They make every device send data at exactly the same moment
Agreed error-checking and acknowledgement rules mean lost or corrupt data is re-sent
They stop any data being sent over long or noisy links
q.why: Reliability comes from agreed rules for error checking and acknowledgement.

q.q: Why does a published protocol give buyers more choice?
o: It fixes one price for all network equipment
Any product that follows it will work with other makers' products
It means only one manufacturer may make each device
It allows each maker to design its own private rules
q.why: A manufacturer following a published protocol knows its product will interoperate, so buyers can mix makes.

q.q: What does OSI stand for?
o: Open Systems Interconnection
Operating Systems Interface
Open Standards Internet
Organised Signal Interchange
q.why: OSI is the Open Systems Interconnection model, published by ISO.

q.q: Which organisation published the OSI model?
o: ITU
ISO
IEEE
IETF
q.why: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) published the OSI reference model.

q.q: Which OSI layer encrypts and compresses data?
o: Transport
Presentation
Session
Data link
q.why: The presentation layer converts formats, encrypts/decrypts and compresses/decompresses.

q.q: Which layers make up the Application set?
o: Session, transport and network
Application, transport and network
Application, presentation and session
Presentation, data link and physical
q.why: The Application set is layers 7 to 5.

q.q: Which layers make up the Transport set?
o: Transport, network, data link and physical
Network, data link and physical only
Session, transport, network and data link
Application, presentation, session and transport
q.why: The Transport set is layers 4 to 1.

q.q: Which OSI layer works out the best route and adds the destination IP address?
o: Transport
Session
Network
Data link
q.why: The network layer handles addressing and routing; transport splits and reassembles packets.

q.q: Which OSI layer splits data into packets and puts them back in order at the destination?
o: Transport
Session
Data link
Network
q.why: The notes warn not to swap them: transport splits and reassembles; network addresses and routes.

q.q: Which OSI layer opens a temporary channel when an application connects to a remote server, and closes it afterwards?
o: Presentation
Application
Session
Transport
q.why: The session layer opens, manages and closes the communication channel.

q.q: Which OSI layer turns each packet into a frame and detects and corrects bit errors?
o: Network
Data link
Transport
Physical
q.why: The data link layer frames bits for the link and handles bit errors.

q.q: Which OSI layer turns bits into voltages, light pulses or radio waves?
o: Data link
Physical
Network
Presentation
q.why: The physical layer converts bits to signals and fixes connectors, voltage levels and timing.

q.q: Why is the OSI model described as a framework?
o: It is a physical layout of cables and switched hubs
It defines the exact hardware every network must use
It replaces all other protocols with one standard
It says what each layer must do but not how it is implemented
q.why: Implementation is left to the designers of hardware, software and protocols.

q.q: On the sending device, in which direction does data pass through the OSI layers?
o: Across from the session layer to the transport layer
Up from the physical layer to the application layer
Down from the application layer to the physical layer
From the network layer outwards in both directions
q.why: Data passes down on the sender and back up on the receiver, each layer undoing its partner's work.

q.q: Which is a benefit of the layered OSI model for fault-finding?
o: Every layer checks the work of all the other layers
Faults can only ever occur at the physical layer
The whole network must be redesigned to fix a fault
Problems can be isolated to the layer where they occur
q.why: Error handling at each layer means problems can be isolated, speeding up fault-finding.

q.q: How does the four-layer TCP/IP model relate to OSI?
o: It removes the transport and network layers altogether
It splits the OSI application layer into four parts
It merges OSI layers 5 to 7 into one and layers 1 to 2 into one
It merges OSI layers 1 to 3 into one and layers 4 to 7 into one
q.why: TCP/IP has application, transport, internet and link layers, merging OSI 5-7 and 1-2.

q.q: In TCP/IP, which protocol puts packets back in the right order at the destination?
o: CSMA/CD
Ethernet
IP
TCP
q.why: TCP numbers the packets and reassembles them in order.

q.q: What job does IP do in TCP/IP?
o: Adds source and destination addresses and moves packets node to node
Checks each packet and asks for lost packets to be re-sent
Splits data into numbered packets and puts them back in order
Listens to the channel and waits until it is free to send
q.why: IP addresses packets and routers forward them hop by hop; numbering and reassembly are TCP's job.

q.q: What is packet switching?
o: Packets are swapped between TCP and IP at each router
A device switches between wired and wireless links
Packets of one message may take different routes to the destination
A switched hub sends each packet to every port in turn
q.why: Under IP, packets are forwarded independently and may travel by different routes.

q.q: What is Ethernet's formal standard number?
o: IEEE 802.15
IEEE 802.3
ISO 9001
IEEE 802.11
q.why: 802.3 is Ethernet; 802.11 is Wi-Fi.

q.q: At which OSI layers does Ethernet work, according to the notes?
o: Data link and network
Network and transport
Physical and transport
Physical and data link
q.why: Ethernet defines cables, plugs and frames, so it sits at the physical and data link layers.

q.q: Which addresses does each Ethernet frame carry?
o: The source and destination MAC addresses
The address of the router and the ISP
The source and destination IP addresses only
The port numbers of the sending and receiving programs
q.why: An Ethernet frame carries source and destination MAC addresses and an error-check value.

q.q: Which part of CSMA/CD means a device listens to the channel before sending?
o: Carrier sense
Back-off
Multiple access
Collision detection
q.why: Carrier sense: listen first and wait if another transmission is in progress.

q.q: What does a device do after a collision under CSMA/CD?
o: Passes the token on to the next device
Waits a fixed time agreed with the other sender
Waits a random time, then tries again
Sends again immediately to avoid a delay
q.why: A random back-off makes a repeat collision unlikely; a fixed wait would make both resend together.

q.q: Under CSMA/CD, what happens to the range of possible waiting times after each further collision?
o: It stays the same
It increases
It is reset to zero
It decreases
q.why: After each further collision the range of possible waiting times is increased.

q.q: Why can token passing never cause collisions?
o: Only the device holding the token may transmit
Each device sends in a random time slot
Data travels in both directions at once
The token encrypts every packet it carries
q.why: With one sender at a time there can be no collisions.

q.q: A network is under heavy load. How do CSMA/CD and token passing compare?
o: Both slow down equally because of collisions
Token passing suffers more collisions; CSMA/CD stays steady
Both speed up because more devices are sending
CSMA/CD suffers more collisions; token passing stays steady
q.why: Under heavy load CSMA/CD has more collisions, while token passing is predictable as each waits its turn.

q.q: What is HTTPS?
o: A version of HTTP that compresses web pages
Web traffic sent over an encrypted SSL/TLS link that also authenticates the site
A certificate issued to the browser by the website
A protocol that splits web pages into numbered packets
q.why: HTTPS is HTTP over SSL/TLS encryption and it authenticates the website.

q.q: What does a digital certificate do?
o: Gives a server a fixed public IP address
Shows that a website contains no viruses
Encrypts every packet sent by a user's browser
Proves a server's identity and carries its public key
q.why: A digital certificate, issued by a trusted certificate authority, proves identity and carries the public key.

q.q: What do Bluetooth devices form when they pair?
o: A WLAN
A MAN
A piconet
A hotspot
q.why: A piconet is Bluetooth's small ad hoc network; a hotspot is a Wi-Fi coverage area.

q.q: What does a device need to join a closed Wi-Fi network?
o: An RJ45 port and an Ethernet cable
A media converter and a fixed IP address
A Bluetooth chip and a pairing passcode
A wireless adapter and the network password
q.why: The adapter sends and receives the radio signals; a closed network needs a password.

q.q: Which is a typical range of a Class 1 Bluetooth device?
o: About 100 m
About 10 m
About 1 m
About 1 km
q.why: Class 1 reaches about 100 m; Class 3 about 10 m.

q.q: Wi-Fi is formally which standard?
o: IEEE 802.11
IEEE 802.3
ISO 7498
IEEE 802.15
q.why: Wi-Fi is 802.11; Ethernet is 802.3.

q.q: What is the typical range of a Wi-Fi access point given in the notes?
o: About 5 km
About 400 m
About 60 to 90 m
About 10 m
q.why: The notes give about 60-90 m, enough for a home and the street outside.

q.q: Why is an open Wi-Fi network a security risk?
o: Its range is too short to be used in a café
Devices must pair with a passcode before joining
Anyone can join and traffic may not be encrypted
It uses a wired connection that can be tapped
q.why: Open networks need no password, and their traffic may not be encrypted.

q.q: What is the main difference in purpose between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth?
o: Wi-Fi joins devices to a network; Bluetooth links devices directly to each other
Wi-Fi links devices directly; Bluetooth joins devices to a network
Wi-Fi is low power; Bluetooth needs much more power
Wi-Fi uses radio waves; Bluetooth uses infrared light
q.why: Both use radio, but Wi-Fi connects to a network through a WAP while Bluetooth is peer-to-peer.

q.q: Why is Bluetooth well suited to wireless earbuds?
o: It needs a wireless access point to connect them
It uses low power and links devices directly over a short range
It carries hundreds of Mbps for high-quality sound
It has a longer range and higher speed than Wi-Fi
q.why: Bluetooth's low power and direct pairing suit wearables and earbuds.

q.q: Which is a similarity between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth?
o: Both need a wireless access point to work
Both are wireless radio protocols with fairly short range
Both create a piconet when devices connect
Both have speeds of hundreds of Mbps
q.why: The notes say a compare answer should include that both are short-range radio protocols.

q.q: What does VoIP do to a caller's voice?
o: Sends it directly to the other phone by Bluetooth
Converts it to text and sends it as a message
Sends it as an analogue signal over the phone network
Digitises it into data packets sent over IP networks
q.why: VoIP turns speech into ordinary data packets sent using IP.

q.q: Which development made VoIP practical for natural conversation?
o: Token passing on ring networks
The invention of the RFID tag
Fast, always-on broadband
Two-dimensional parity checking
q.why: Packets must arrive fast enough for real-time talk, which fast always-on broadband allows.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of VoIP?
o: Call quality drops when the connection is congested
Calls between internet users are very expensive
Calls cannot be recorded or forwarded as email
It can only be used from a VoIP desk phone
q.why: Congestion causes lag, jitter and dropped words, and calls fail if the internet goes down.

q.q: Why can VoIP easily offer features such as voicemail sent as email and conference calls?
o: Every VoIP phone has its own built-in mail server
Calls are just data, so they can be handled like other data
VoIP uses the traditional telephone exchange for every call
VoIP calls are sent as analogue signals that are easy to copy
q.why: Because calls are just data, extra features come easily.

q.q: How is a passive RFID tag powered?
o: By the radio waves from the reader
By the item it is attached to
By its own built-in battery
By a small solar panel on the tag
q.why: Passive tags have no battery and draw energy from the reader's signal.

q.q: Compared with a passive RFID tag, what does an active tag have?
o: A barcode printed on it as a backup
A need for line of sight to the reader
No chip, so it is cheaper and smaller
Its own power supply and a much longer read range
q.why: Active tags have their own power, so they can be read from much further away.

q.q: Which is an advantage of RFID over barcodes?
o: No line of sight is needed and many tags can be read at once
RFID tags must be printed on the outside of the packaging
Each RFID tag is cheaper to make than a printed barcode
RFID data is read-only, so it cannot be changed
q.why: RFID reads through packaging, many at a time; barcodes win only on cost.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a barcode over an RFID tag?
o: It holds more data than a tag
It can be rewritten and reused
It is almost free to print
It can be read without line of sight
q.why: Barcodes are cheap; RFID tags cost more and need readers.

q.q: A warehouse wants to check every item on a pallet in seconds as it passes through a doorway. Which technology suits this best?
o: VoIP, since each item can report its stock level by call
Barcodes, since each must be lined up with the scanner
Bluetooth, since each item must be paired with a phone
RFID tags, since many can be read at once without line of sight
q.why: RFID reads a whole pallet automatically in seconds.

q.q: Which is the best definition of bandwidth?
o: The total length of cable used in a network
The number of users connected to a network at once
The capacity of a channel, such as the range of frequencies it can carry
A fast internet connection that is permanently connected
q.why: Bandwidth is capacity, measured in hertz or bits per second; always-on fast access describes broadband.

q.q: What makes a connection broadband in the technical sense?
o: It carries several signals on different frequencies at once
It always uses wireless radio links
It always uses fibre optic cable to the premises
It has a static IP address
q.why: Broadband is wide-bandwidth transmission, carrying many signals at once on different frequencies.

q.q: In which units can bandwidth be measured?
o: Hertz, or bits per second
Bytes, or kilobytes
Metres, or kilometres
Packets, or frames
q.why: Bandwidth is a frequency range in Hz or a data rate in bps.

q.q: How long does a 250 MB file take to transfer at 20 Mbps (1 MB = 8 Mb)?
q.why: 250 x 8 = 2000 Mb; 2000 / 20 = 100 s. 12.5 s comes from forgetting to multiply by 8.

q.q: How long does a 40 MB file take to download at 8 Mbps (1 MB = 8 Mb)?
o: 8 s
5 s
q.why: 40 x 8 = 320 Mb; 320 / 8 = 40 s. 5 s comes from not converting bytes to bits.

q.q: How does DSL broadband share a copper phone line with voice calls?
o: It compresses voice calls into the data stream
It sends data at frequencies above those used for voice
It turns off the phone service while data is sent
It sends voice and data in turns, one packet each
q.why: Voice and data use different frequency bands, so they share the line without interfering.

q.q: What does a line advertised as '64k' mean?
o: It can store 64 KB of data
It passes a range of 64 kHz
It can carry 64 calls at once
Its maximum data rate is 64 kbps
q.why: Bandwidth quoted as line speed: 64k means 64 kbps.

q.q: How did old dial-up internet differ from broadband?
o: It used Wi-Fi rather than the telephone line
It tied up the phone line and ran at about 56 kbps
It used fibre optic cable right into the premises
It was always on and ran at hundreds of Mbps
q.why: Dial-up blocked the phone line and ran at 56 kbps; broadband is always on and fast.

q.q: Which transmission medium is immune to electrical interference?
o: Shielded twisted pair
Fibre optic cable
Unshielded twisted pair
Coaxial cable
q.why: Fibre carries light, not electrical signals; shielding only reduces interference on copper.

q.q: What is the approximate maximum run length of twisted pair Ethernet cable?
o: 10 km
1 km
q.why: Twisted pair carries signals about 100 m per run.

q.q: Why are the strands in a fibre optic cable used in pairs or bundles?
o: A single strand is too fragile to carry light
Each strand can carry only one signal at a time
One strand carries light and the other electricity
Light travels in only one direction along a strand
q.why: Separate strands (or bundles) carry outgoing and returning pulses.

q.q: What does the shielding in STP cable do?
o: Carries the return signal in the other direction
Protects the data from electrical interference
Keeps the light inside the glass strand
Increases the run length to several kilometres
q.why: STP's shielding protects data from corruption in electrically noisy places.

q.q: What is the purpose of the cladding in a fibre optic cable?
o: To carry the returning light pulses
To shield the copper from electrical interference
To keep the light inside the glass strand
To convert light into electrical signals
q.why: Cladding surrounds each strand and keeps the light in the glass.

q.q: Why are the wires in UTP cable twisted round each other?
o: To let one pair carry data in both directions at once
To make the cable stiffer and easier to install
To let the cable carry light as well as electricity
To cancel much of the electrical interference and reduce signal loss
q.why: Twisting cancels interference and reduces signal loss.

q.q: How is data carried along a fibre optic cable?
o: As voltages on pairs of twisted copper wires
As radio waves inside a shielded tube
As electrical signals along a central copper conductor
As modulated pulses of light along fine glass strands
q.why: Fibre carries pulses of light in glass; copper carries electrical signals.

q.q: A factory with heavy electrical machinery needs copper cabling between its machines and a nearby switch. Which cable is best?
o: Old telephone cable
Bluetooth link
Shielded twisted pair
Unshielded twisted pair
q.why: STP's shielding suits electrically noisy places such as factories.

q.q: Two school buildings are 400 m apart. Which medium is the best choice to link them by cable?
o: Shielded twisted pair, as it reaches 1 km
Fibre optic, as it travels far without a repeater
Coaxial cable, as it is used for long distances
Unshielded twisted pair, as it is cheapest
q.why: Twisted pair is limited to about 100 m; fibre travels kilometres without a repeater.

q.q: Which is a drawback of fibre optic cable?
o: It can only carry signals about 100 m
It picks up interference from nearby machinery
It is expensive and needs specialist installation and joining
It has a lower bandwidth than coaxial cable
q.why: Fibre's drawbacks are cost and specialist installation.

q.q: Which medium is hardest to intercept without being detected?
o: Coaxial cable
Fibre optic
Wi-Fi
Twisted pair
q.why: Tapping fibre means cutting or bending it, which disturbs the light and is easily detected.

q.q: Why does each pupil's Wi-Fi speed fall when many pupils connect to one access point?
o: Each pupil's device uses a different protocol
Radio waves travel more slowly when there are more users
The access point's bandwidth is shared between them
Encryption stops working when many users join
q.why: Wireless capacity is shared by all users of an access point.

q.q: Which measure most improves the security of a wireless network?
o: Using an open network so devices connect quickly
Moving the access point outside the building
Adding a repeater to extend the range
Strong encryption such as WPA3 and a password
q.why: Encryption stops intercepted data being read, and a password closes the network.

q.q: Why is wireless the least secure transmission medium?
o: Wireless signals carry no addresses, so they cannot be checked
Wireless data must pass through every other device on the network
Radio waves can only be encrypted by fibre optic links
Radio waves spread beyond the building, so anyone in range can capture them
q.why: Anyone within range can receive the signal unless it is encrypted.

q.q: What does an attacker need in order to intercept data on metal cable?
o: Physical access to the cable or switch
Only to be within radio range of the building
A media converter to turn the light into electricity
The MAC address of every device on the network
q.why: Copper can be tapped, but only with physical access to the cable or switch.

q.q: Rank the media from largest to smallest volume of data transfer.
o: Wireless, then fibre, then metal cable
Fibre, then wireless, then metal cable
Metal cable, then fibre, then wireless
Fibre, then metal cable, then wireless
q.why: The notes summarise volume as fibre > metal > wireless, as wireless capacity is shared and variable.

q.q: Why does fibre optic have far more bandwidth than metal cable?
o: It carries electrical signals at a higher voltage
It is shared by all users within range
It uses a very wide range of light frequencies
It is twisted to cancel out interference
q.why: Fibre's wide range of light frequencies gives far more bandwidth; copper is limited by the wire's electrical properties.

q.q: A 6-mark question asks whether metal cable or wireless is better for data security. What does a top-band answer need?
o: An evaluation of both media for cost, volume and bandwidth
A table of facts about both media covering cost, speed and security
Both media described, both evaluated for security only, and a clear judgement
A description of the more secure medium only, with a judgement
q.why: Banded answers describe both, evaluate both against the named criterion only, and end with a judgement.

q.q: Which comparison of metal cable and wireless is correct?
o: Cable can be intercepted by anyone in range; wireless needs physical access
Cable is shared by all users; wireless gives each device a dedicated link
Cable gives each device a steady dedicated link; wireless is shared and varies
Cable is protected by MAC filtering; wireless by physical security of rooms
q.why: A cable gives a dedicated link per device; wireless capacity is shared by all users of the access point.

q.q: With even parity, what must be true of each byte?
o: It contains an even number of 0s
Its denary value is an even number
Its leftmost bit is always 0
It contains an even number of 1s
q.why: The parity bit is set so the byte has an even number of 1s.

q.q: Using even parity with the parity bit on the left, what is the byte for the 7-bit code 101 1001?
q.why: 101 1001 has four 1s, already even, so the parity bit is 0.

q.q: Using odd parity with the parity bit on the left, what is the byte for the 7-bit code 100 0011 (letter C)?
q.why: 100 0011 has three 1s, already odd, so the parity bit is 0.

q.q: Using even parity with the parity bit on the left, what is the byte for the 7-bit code 101 0100 (letter T)?
q.why: 101 0100 has three 1s, so a parity bit of 1 makes four, which is even.

q.q: Which error does a single parity bit fail to detect?
o: Three bits flipped in the same byte
Two bits flipped in the same byte
The parity bit itself flipped
One data bit flipped in the byte
q.why: Two flips leave the count of 1s with the same parity, so the error is missed.

q.q: A byte sent with even parity as 1001 1010 has its first and last bits flipped. What happens?
o: The byte is corrected automatically by the receiver
The error is not detected, because the parity is still even
The error is detected, because the parity bit changed
The error is detected, because the parity becomes odd
q.why: 0001 1011 still has four 1s, so a double error is missed.

q.q: A byte is sent with even parity. The receiver gets 0110 1001. What should it conclude?
o: No error is detected, because the last bit is 1
An error is detected, because there are five 1s
No error is detected, because there are four 1s
An error is detected, because the parity bit is 0
q.why: 0110 1001 has four 1s, which matches even parity.

q.q: A byte is sent with odd parity. Which received byte shows an error has been detected?
q.why: 1100 0011 has four 1s, which is even, so it fails an odd parity check; the others each have an odd number.

q.q: How does two-dimensional (block) parity locate a single flipped bit?
o: The receiver counts the bytes in the block
The failing row and the failing column cross at the faulty bit
The receiver re-sends the whole block and compares the two
The failing row is divided by a fixed binary number
q.why: Row parity and column parity together pinpoint the bit, which is then flipped back.

q.q: Why does 7-bit ASCII leave a bit free for parity?
o: The leftmost bit of ASCII is always 1, so it can be reused
Each character needs eight bits, so a ninth is added for parity
Each character needs only seven bits, leaving the eighth bit of the byte spare
ASCII uses only even numbers, so the last bit is spare
q.why: 7-bit ASCII leaves the leftmost bit of each byte free to become the parity bit.

q.q: Which is a weakness of using a single parity bit?
o: It adds a whole extra byte to every byte sent
It cannot detect a single flipped bit
It is slow and complex to calculate in hardware
It cannot show which bit is wrong, so it cannot correct the error
q.why: A single parity bit detects odd numbers of errors but cannot locate them; it is simple and only one bit per byte.

q.q: What does a receiver do in echo checking?
o: Divides the data by a fixed binary number
Sends an exact copy of the received data back to the sender
Counts the 1s in each byte and checks the parity
Adds up the bytes and compares the total with a checksum
q.why: The sender then compares the echoed copy with the original it holds.

q.q: In a CRC, what is sent with the data?
o: A full copy of the data sent back by the receiver
The remainder of dividing the block by a fixed binary number
The total of all the bytes in the block
The quotient of dividing the block by a fixed binary number
q.why: The remainder is the check value appended to the block.

q.q: Which error detection method doubles the amount of data sent?
o: Parity bits
Checksums
CRC
Echo checking
q.why: Everything travels twice: out and back.

q.q: Bytes 10, 20 and 30 are sent with an additive checksum MOD 256. What is the checksum?
q.why: 10 + 20 + 30 = 60, which is below 256, so the remainder is 60.

q.q: Bytes 200, 100 and 50 are sent with an additive checksum MOD 256. What is the checksum?
In a CRC, the receiver divides the received block (with its check value) by the generator. What does a remainder of zero mean?
o: The generator number was wrong
The block must be re-transmitted
An error was found and corrected
No error was detected
q.why: A zero remainder means no error was detected; any other value means the data changed.

q.q: Why do Ethernet and Wi-Fi frames carry a CRC rather than a single parity bit?
o: CRC detects multiple errors, including burst errors
CRC needs no extra bits to be sent with the data
CRC sends a full copy of the frame back to the sender
CRC is simpler to calculate than parity
q.why: CRC catches multiple and burst errors, which parity can miss.

q.q: Which is a weakness of echo checking?
o: Errors that cancel out in the sum are missed
It can only detect an odd number of flipped bits
A corrupted echo can cause correct data to be re-sent needlessly
It needs a complex division done in hardware
q.why: If the echo is corrupted on the way back, the sender re-sends data that was in fact fine.
